newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-MORGAN SHATTERS RECORD AT THE TRADITION, WINS BY SIX SHOTS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MORGAN SHATTERS RECORD AT THE TRADITION, WINS BY SIX SHOTS.

text.p: Gil Morgan shattered the tournament record, completed a wire-to-wire victory and captured his first major championship Sunday with a six-shot triumph at The Tradition.
Morgan had a 5-under-par 67 -- his fourth straight round in the 60s -- for a 72-hole total of 22-under 266.

He broke the tournament record of 269, set by Tom Shaw in 1993, and posted the second-lowest score in any of the Senior PGA Tour's four major championships. The six-stroke margin also was the largest in tournament history.

"I'm very excited about the win," said Morgan. "Obviously, things have changed with the ageing process and all that stuff. But to win a major championship on the Senior Tour is probably the highlight of a senior player's career.
"Obviously, every win is nice and enjoyable, but we all look toward, from a record book standpoint, the major championships, see if you can get your name in the book."
Morgan, who also eclipsed the 54-hole tournament mark, finished with a flourish, eagling the par-5 18th hole for a six-stroke victory over Japan's Isao Aoki, who had a final-round 68.
"Gil played too well," said Aoki, who also finished second here in 1995. "He was very good. I made too many bogeys this week, 11 bogeys."
John Jacobs was third at 14-under 274, followed by Larry Gilbert at 276 and Jay Sigel at 277.

The 50-year-old Morgan joined the Senior Tour last September and won the Ralphs Senior Classic one week later. This was his first victory this year and the $180,000 first prize -- which equalled the largest of his career -- moved him into second place on the 1997 money list with $415,204.
Morgan, a doctor of optometry, said he may have sealed the win on Sunday's first hole. He saved par while Aoki missed a short birdie putt.
"If he made that and I made bogey, I don't know what would have happened," Morgan said. "It could have gone any way at that point in time.

"My game plan was not to try to make too many mistakes, obviously, and I succeeded pretty much in doing that. I made a few glitches out there, but I recovered from almost all of them with no worse than par.
"So from that standpoint, I felt like I accomplished my goals as far as playing the golf course.
"Nobody seemed to put very much pressure on me early," he added, "so that helped a little bit, too. I just kept playing and I was able to make a couple of birdies on the front."

Morgan had seven wins on the PGA Tour, but never captured a major. He had his chances, leading the 1976 PGA Championship by four shots and sitting atop the leaderboard midway through the 1984 Masters.
Morgan also was the first player in U.S. Open history to reach 10 under par, climbing to 12 under at Pebble Beach in 1992 before a final-round 81 dropped him to a 13th-place tie.
There was no collapse here. Morgan played the last 33 holes without a bogey, had only three for the tournament and has strung together eight consecutive rounds below par.
Jack Nicklaus, the four-time and defending champion of this event, had a 27-under 261 to win the 1990 Senior Players Championship -- the lowest total in a Senior major.
Nicklaus was in contention for a record fifth title after an opening-round 67. But he posted rounds of 74-75-73 and tied for 25th at 1-over 289 on the course he designed.

Many of the other big names on the Senior Tour also struggled this weekend. Hale Irwin was 16 strokes behind at 6-under 282, David Graham, the leading money-winner who was coming off a victory at last week's Dominion, shot a 2-under 70 in the final round to finish at 1-under 287.
Former champion Ray Floyd was one shot better than Graham, but Lee Trevino, who won this event in 1992, was a whopping 23 strokes back at 289.
